Computational Linguistics 2025NLG evaluation · Survey

LLM-based NLG Evaluation: Current Status and Challenges

Mingqi Gao*, Xinyu Hu*, Xunjian Yin, Jie Ruan, Xiao Pu, Xiaojun Wan

Paper ↗arXiv ↗

LLMs can evaluate generated text in several distinct ways. This survey organizes the methods and explains the reliability, cost, and control trade-offs behind each choice.

01 / The research question

Choosing an evaluator also chooses what quality means

A generated answer can be fluent, relevant, complete, and factually wrong at the same time. This makes NLG evaluation unlike checking a single label: valid outputs differ, and different users may value different qualities. The survey’s organizing question is not whether an LLM can emit a plausible score. It is how the score is obtained, what information supports it, and which assumptions are hidden inside the evaluation procedure.

For example, likelihood-based scoring asks whether text is probable under a model, while a prompted judge is asked to apply an explicit rubric. A fine-tuned evaluator learns from examples of judgments; human–LLM collaboration keeps people involved in defining criteria or inspecting assessments. These approaches can use the same underlying language model and still measure different things. The four-part taxonomy makes those design choices visible rather than grouping every use of an LLM under one metric label.

02 / Inside the method

The taxonomy separates signals, interfaces, and supervision

LLM-derived metrics extract evaluation signals from model representations or generation probabilities. Their numerical outputs are convenient, but a score’s relation to a chosen quality dimension may be indirect. Prompted evaluation supplies task instructions and criteria, then requests scores, pairwise comparisons, rankings, answers to evaluation questions, or error analyses. Changing the output format changes the decision being asked of the model; a preference between two answers is not automatically a calibrated absolute rating.

Fine-tuning moves part of the evaluation design into training data. Important differences include who produces the labels, whether explanations are included, whether references are required, and whether criteria can vary at inference. The final survey also distinguishes human-guided LLM evaluation from LLM-assisted human evaluation. People may define or refine rubrics for a model, while a model may propose critiques or test cases for a human to review. These are different divisions of work, with different costs and failure modes.

  1. 01

    Organize the approaches

    Group the literature into LLM-derived metrics, prompting, fine-tuning, and human–LLM collaborative evaluation.

  2. 02

    Compare evaluation designs

    Examine scoring, pairwise comparison, ranking, Boolean questions, and error analysis, alongside training data and evaluator outputs.

  3. 03

    Identify unresolved problems

    Analyze reliability, robustness, bias, interpretability, and how human participation can support evaluation quality.

03 / Reading the evidence

Useful evaluation needs its own evaluation

  • 4 paradigms

    A shared taxonomy

    A common framework connects methods that extract model signals, prompt general models, train evaluators, or combine human and model judgments.

  • Bias persists

    Reliability requires validation

    The surveyed literature reports sensitivity to presentation order, output length, and model preferences, limiting unqualified trust in LLM judgments.

Because this is a survey, its contribution is a structured synthesis rather than a new shared leaderboard experiment. The literature documents cases where prompted judges favor a response’s presentation position, length, or stylistic resemblance to model-generated text. Fine-tuning can address some behaviors, but synthetic evaluation data can also carry the teacher model’s biases into a smaller evaluator. An explanation can expose the judge’s stated reasoning without guaranteeing that the reasoning is faithful or correct.

A practical implication is to validate the evaluator against the decision it will actually support. If the aim is system ranking, inspect agreement at that level; if the aim is identifying factual errors in individual answers, system-level correlation is insufficient. Criteria, model versions, input formats, and human reference judgments all belong in that validation. The survey supports choosing an approach with explicit trade-offs, rather than interpreting the flexibility of natural-language judging as evidence that evaluation has become a solved problem.

Scope. This is a synthesis of the literature available at publication, not a benchmark establishing a universal best evaluator. Reported strengths depend on tasks, criteria, models, and validation data. Read the study ↗

Read the abstract

Evaluating natural language generation (NLG) is a vital but challenging problem in natural language processing. Traditional evaluation metrics mainly capturing content (e.g., n-gram) overlap between system outputs and references are far from satisfactory, and large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated great potential in NLG evaluation in recent years. Various automatic evaluation methods based on LLMs have been proposed, including metrics derived from LLMs, prompting LLMs, fine-tuning LLMs, and human–LLM collaborative evaluation. In this survey, we first give a taxonomy of LLM-based NLG evaluation methods, and discuss their pros and cons, respectively. Lastly, we discuss several open problems in this area and point out future research directions.
